Industry News: No GPU left behind: Unlocking Efficiency with Co-located vLLM in TRL

📅 03 Jun 2025 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2792 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that TRL supports training LLMs using GRPO, an online learning algorithm recently introduced in the DeepSeekMath paper.
  • Recent findings suggest that this makes generation a critical step in the training loop — and also a major bottleneck.
  • Industry observers note that before TRL v0.18.0, vLLM was only supported in server mode, running as a separate process on different GPUs from the training job.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that TRL supports training LLMs using GRPO, an online learning algorithm recently introduced in the DeepSeekMath paper. In GRPO, the model learns from its own outputs: it generates responses during training, receives feedback, and uses that feedback to improve itself over time.

Recent findings suggest that this makes generation a critical step in the training loop — and also a major bottleneck. To speed up generation, TRL integrates with vLLM. This combination lets you train powerful models more efficiently in GRPO setup. However, there’s a catch.

Industry observers note that before TRL v0.18.0, vLLM was only supported in server mode, running as a separate process on different GPUs from the training job. It communicated with the training script over HTTP, which made the setup modular and easy to use — but also introduced GPU inefficiencies.

This “ping-pong” between training and generation causes:.

Sources indicate that in online learning methods like GRPO — where generation happens constantly — this inefficiency becomes even more painful. You spend more on hardware, but don't get the performance you'd expect.

So, the key question becomes: Can we share the same GPUs for both training and generation, instead of separating them?

Industry observers note that the main issue was that training and inference ran on separate GPUs, leading to idle time and underutilization. The natural solution? Run both on the same GPUs. Instead of having vLLM operate as a standalone server in its own process and devices, what if vLLM could run alongside the training code, within the same distributed process group? This would let us launch a single distributed job where training and inference share the same devices, switching between tasks efficiently without wasting resources.

It has been revealed that this approach is what we refer to as colocation. Training and inference are co-located on the same GPUs and coordinated via the same process group, allowing them to take turns smoothly — no extra hardware needed.

Industry observers note that previously, this wasn’t possible in TRL, which relied on vLLM as an external HTTP server. That changed with our PR #3394, which added support for vLLM’s external launcher and true integration into the training process.

In a recent development, unified Execution: By embedding vLLM in the same process group, both training and inference tasks can share the same GPUs, taking turns instead of waiting on each other. This reduces idle time and boosts overall efficiency.

Skip HTTP Communication: No need for REST API calls or networking — vLLM runs inline with the training loop, avoiding overhead and latency.

Torchrun Compatibility: Works seamlessly with torchrun, so it's easy to scale across nodes with minimal config changes.

TP and DP Support: Compatible with Tensor Parallelism and Data Parallelism, making it suitable for large-scale training runs.

In a recent development, SPMD Execution Pattern: Uses a Single Program, Multiple Data (SPMD) model, where each GPU runs its own instance of the engine in sync. Ideal for distributed multi-GPU, multi-node setups.

Simplified Deployment: You no longer need to maintain a separate server script — vLLM is launched and controlled directly inside your training job.

Enhanced Throughput: By avoiding idle GPUs and eliminating inter-process communication, the system delivers faster training and generation, especially crucial in online learning setups like GRPO.

Robust Inter-process Communication: This is more robust because it avoids the complexity of setting up distributed process groups between independent processes, as required in server mode.

Thanks to this feature, co-located training and inference is no longer a hack — it’s now first-class, scalable, and production-ready.

The shift from server TRL to co-located TRL is all about smarter GPU usage. The diagram below shows the difference:.

In the server TRL setup, training and inference run on separate GPUs. For example:.

During training steps, GPU 3 sits idle. During generation steps (inference), GPUs 0–2 are idle while GPU 3 generates outputs.

It has been revealed that in contrast, the co-located TRL setup runs both training and vLLM on the same GPUs. Each GPU:.

Training and inference take turns using the GPU’s resources — no need for dedicated devices or separate processes.

Instead of launching vLLM as a server, the trainer now releases vLLM in-process using the external launcher, as shown below:.

Co-located vLLM respects the torch.distributed process group and rank structure. This allows vLLM to be initialized alongside training without conflict and makes TP/DP setups work seamlessly:.

Co-located vLLM no longer relies on REST APIs — it runs directly in memory and communicates via native Python calls:.

To use this setup, simply set vllm_mode="colocate" in your GRPO configuration:.

Note: Depending on the model size and the overall GPU memory requirements for training, you may need to adjust the vllm_gpu_memory_utilization parameter in GRPOConfig to avoid underutilization or out-of-memory errors.

To measure the impact of colocation, we ran a series of experiments comparing the traditional server mode (where vLLM runs on a separate GPU as a standalone server) with the new co-locate mode (where training and inference share the same GPUs).

In server mode, only 7 GPUs are used for training because 1 GPU is fully dedicated to the vLLM inference server.

In co-locate mode, all 8 GPUs are used for training — increasing the effective batch size by default.

Industry observers note that to ensure a fair comparison, we normalized throughput in server mode by a factor of 8/7. This adjustment accounts for the greater training capacity in co-locate mode and allows us to compare the two setups under equal training conditions.

In a recent development, when training large models like Qwen2.5-Math-72B, it's important to use the right strategies to make training efficient, scalable, and stable across many GPUs and nodes. In our setup, we combined co-located vLLM with several key optimizations to make this work efficiently.

Sources indicate that when using co-located training, managing GPU memory is crucial so that both training and inference can run smoothly on the same devices. To support this, we added vLLM’s sleep() API into the GRPO training loop.

According to recent reports, the sleep() function temporarily pauses the vLLM engine and frees up GPU memory. It supports two levels:.

Recent findings suggest that level 1: Unloads model weights from GPU (keeps them in CPU memory) and clears the KV cache. Useful when the same model will be reused soon.

Industry observers note that level 2: Unloads both model weights and KV cache entirely. Best for scenarios where the model will change or won’t be reused right away.

In GRPO, the model is updated after every step — so we use Level 2 sleep.

This small addition makes a substantial difference in enabling smooth and scalable co-located training.

To train large models like Qwen2.5-72B, we rely on DeepSpeed ZeRO Stage 3, the same setup used in plain TRL.

ZeRO helps scale large models by distributing memory across GPUs. Stage 3 goes further by partitioning:.

It has been revealed that this is essential for models that can’t fit on a single GPU. With ZeRO Stage 3, each GPU handles only a portion of the model.

"offload_optimizer": {"device": "cpu"} Moves optimizer states to CPU to free GPU memory — critical in co-located setups.

"overlap_comm": true Enables communication overlap with computation, speeding up training.

"contiguous_gradients": true Allocates gradients in a single memory block, improving memory access and reducing fragmentation.

These optimizations help train 72B models efficiently, and ensure colocation remains stable under tight memory constraints.

Industry observers note that as recommended in TRL, we use Accelerate, a lightweight library that simplifies distributed training. It handles:.

This makes the setup clean, scalable, and easy to maintain.

Recent findings suggest that even with 4 fewer GPUs, the co-locate setup is ~1.26× faster than plain TRL. This highlights the effectiveness of smarter GPU sharing and memory cleanup using sleep().

Training reward plots for co-locate and plain setups are nearly identical, demonstrating that:.

Recent findings suggest that we evaluated three models: Base model, Co-locate-trained model, Plain-trained model on the Math500 benchmark. Both trained models outperform the base, and the co-locate model performs on par with the plain-trained model — confirming that colocation does not compromise downstream performance.

Through our work on scaling GRPO training with co-located vLLM, we've faced several critical challenges and learned key lessons about efficiency, flexibility, and system design when training large models.

Tensor Parallelism Bug in vLLM ≥ 0.8.0. Tensor Parallelism (TP) with external_launcher stopped working in vLLM version 0.8.0 and above. This was tracked under Glitch #15895. To identify the breaking point, we followed the approach described in this vLLM developer blog post, which provides wheels for every commit. After bisecting, we identified the breaking commit as cc10281. The root cause was determinism — the newer versions required explicitly setting the random seed. Once the seed was set, the issue went away.

It has been revealed that level 2 Sleep Buffer Bug. Initially, level 2 sleep didn’t work correctly when we tried to reload weights using load_weights. This issue was tracked in Issue #16564. The problem was that model buffers (like running mean/var in BatchNorm) weren’t restored after waking up from sleep. The fix came with PR #16889, which added logic to explicitly restore buffers when waking up from level 2 sleep. We now keep a copy of the original buffers and manually reapply them after loading latest weights.

Sources indicate that segmentation Fault on Exit. There’s still an open problem with vLLM sleep causing a segmentation fault at the end of training when closing processes. This was reported in Issue #16993. This crash happens during shutdown but does not break training itself, so we were able to complete all demos and experiments shared in this blog. However, we’re waiting for an official fix before integrating sleep() fully into TRL upstream.

These challenges were not blockers, but they required careful debugging, version control, and a deeper understanding of how vLLM manages memory and parallelism under the hood.

Sources indicate that co-located inference dramatically improves GPU utilization. By allowing training and generation to share the same GPUs, we eliminate idle time and reduce hardware requirements — achieving higher throughput even with fewer GPUs.

Sources indicate that vLLM's sleep() feature is essential for large-scale colocation. It enables fine-grained control over memory usage, allowing training to fully reclaim GPU memory between generation steps — a key enabler for models like Qwen2.5-72B.

DeepSpeed ZeRO Stage 3 is essential for training large models. It allows extremely large networks to fit into memory by distributing model weights, gradients, and optimizer states across multiple GPUs. In our experience, enabling contiguous_gradients helped reduce memory fragmentation, while offloading the optimizer to the CPU freed up critical GPU memory — both of which were especially helpful in colocated setups.

Colocation is powerful but comes with trade-offs. It works best when GPU memory is carefully managed, often requiring manual tuning of memory usage parameters like vllm_gpu_memory_utilization. While it offers clear throughput benefits and reduces idle GPU time, colocation may not be ideal for models with tight memory budgets or when memory fragmentation is not well controlled. When done right, though, it unlocks significant efficiency gains.

It has been revealed that TP/DP compatibility, Accelerate, and torchrun support make deployment seamless. Despite the complexity of the underlying architecture, the entire system can be launched and scaled with standard distributed tools.

Co-located training maintains model quality. Across multiple benchmarks (Math500, AIME24), co-located and plain setups produced comparable results, validating that performance isn’t sacrificed for efficiency.

This blog post explored how co-locating vLLM with GRPO training unlocks significant efficiency gains when training large language models — including models as large as Qwen2.5-72B.

Recent findings suggest that traditionally, TRL only supported vLLM in server mode, which required separate processes and GPUs for inference, leading to wasted compute and idle time. With the introduction of vLLM’s external launcher and the colocation PR in TRL PR #3394, we can now run training and inference within the same distributed process group, on the same GPUs, with full support for TP, DP, and Accelerate.

In a recent development, while challenges remain — such as version-specific vLLM bugs and edge cases such as with sleep() — the overall results show that co-located GRPO is a practical, scalable solution for training large models efficiently. We’re excited to continue refining this setup, integrating features like FSDP, and pushing the limits of large model training — making it faster, cheaper, and more accessible for everyone building the next generation of LLMs.

arXiv:2611.34457v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent video generators produce realistic videos, yet controlling how scenes unfold remains challenging. Structural proxies, such as animated 3D blockouts, guide generation by specifying scene layout, motion, camera behavior, and event order. However, these coarse inputs leave details unspecified and may contain artifacts that should not be reproduced. Successful proxy-guided generation must therefore Preserve intended structure, Complete missing content and correct proxy artifacts, and Bind text, image, and audio conditions to the right entities and events. We introduce ProxyGenBench to study these interacting requirements, with 312 evaluation cases from 60 scenes across three scene tasks and controlled variations in proxy fidelity, text detail, and multimodal inputs. We evaluate five video generators using verified, case-specific checklists. Experiments show that proxies improve spatiotemporal control, but greater proxy detail can coincide with poorer completion, while strong structural adherence does not ensure correct binding.

arXiv:2611.34435v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Modern video generators excel at producing visually plausible futures guided by text and image prompts. Yet their emphasis on semantic plausibility does not guarantee fidelity to the physical consequences of specific actions. Action-conditioned world models (ACWMs), in contrast, aim to simulate how the world responds to robot actions, enabling scalable policy evaluation and improvement without costly real-world rollouts. The challenge is not merely to generate a plausible future, but to predict what follows from a specific physical action. As video priors grow stronger, we ask how little adaptation is truly needed to bridge this gap. We introduce Dianjing, a minimal recipe that preserves and unlocks the capabilities of strong video priors through unified physical action conditioning, training concentrated at the high noise levels where motion and layout, and thus the consequences of actions, are decided, and native history conditioning. Built upon MiniMax H3, a 33B video foundation model, Dianjing freezes the pretrained backbone and trains only 0.34% of its parameters using approximately 65 hours of robot video across two embodiments, without additional robot-specific pretraining or camera calibration. Controlled ablations show that where training is allocated across noise levels matters more than how actions enter the network. On WorldOracle, which evaluates predictions against paired real-world executions, Dianjing achieves the best scores on four of the five evaluation tracks and ranks second on AgiBot-Long. Our findings suggest that strong video priors already bring us most of the way to world modeling; lightweight physical action grounding can unlock their potential for real-world prediction.

Early results from pioneering works have demonstrated that auto-differentiable NMS models can greatly reduce NMS model calibration time while achieving comparable accuracy compared to traditional calibration methods. The efficient gradient-based optimizers have enabled calibration of increasingly sophisticated human models with a large number of parameters, which seek to narrow the gap between simulation and reality. Several modules have been evaluated separately in different studies, but have never been directly compared within the same study. In this work, these modules are compared on the same differentiable upper limb model with a 3-DoF shoulder, a 2-DoF elbow, and 11 superficial and 5 deep muscles in the calibration to find an optimal pipeline for improving model accuracy. The considered modules include muscle synergy, learnable bone parameters, optimizable geometry of wrap objects, and constraint torque of the differentiable arm model. To evaluate the effect and interplay between the modules on calibration accuracy, one or more modules were used in each of 16 calibration configurations, which were compared in terms of the error between two joint torques calculated by the forward and inverse dynamics with the calibrated model on 9 distinctive testing movements across 4 subjects. Results showed that torque loss was reduced by 23.6% on average using muscle synergy extrapolation to estimate deep muscle activities, and by 10.9% on average through bone dynamic parameter optimization, which are both recommended to be incorporated in the calibration.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.34416v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Robots executing tasks in partially observed environments must resolve uncertainty while operating with incomplete skills. Inspired by human curiosity, we investigate how robots can formulate task-relevant hypotheses, seek evidence, and acquire missing skills during task execution. We propose CHASE, a Curiosity-guided Harness for Acquiring Skills from Evidence, which operationalizes curiosity as selecting investigations that resolve task uncertainty and expand executable capabilities. Four modules connect dynamic scene understanding, hypothesis-driven planning, on-demand skill acquisition, and verified execution. The planner balances information value, skill reuse, and acquisition/execution cost. Missing skills trigger bounded exploration, learning from verified segments, and held-out admission during acquisition; separate checks verify physical effects and acquired evidence. Newly admitted skills expand the executable investigation set, closing the loop between resolving uncertainty and acquiring capabilities. Simulation and real-robot experiments evaluate investigation, skill acquisition, and task execution. CHASE achieves 50-80% task success under combined information and capability gaps, with 70-90% evidence resolution.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, we introduce SmolVLA, a compact (450M), open-source Vision-Language-Action model for robotics that runs on consumer hardware.

Recent findings suggest that over the past few years, Transformers have driven remarkable progress in AI, from language models capable of human-like reasoning to multimodal systems that understand both images and text. However, in real-world robotics, advancements have been much slower. Robots still struggle to generalize across diverse objects, environments, and tasks. This limited progress stems from a lack of high-quality, diverse data and the absence of models that can reason and act like humans in the physical world.

It has been revealed that in response to these challenges, the field has recently turned to vision-language-action (VLA) models, which aim to unify perception, language understanding, and action prediction within a single architecture. VLAs typically take as input raw visual observations and natural language instructions, and output corresponding robot actions. While promising, much of the recent progress in VLAs remains locked behind proprietary models trained on large-scale private datasets, often requiring costly hardware setups and extensive engineering resources. As a result, the broader robotics research community faces significant barriers in reproducing and building upon these models.

SmolVLA addresses this gap by offering an open-source, compact, and efficient VLA model that can be trained on consumer-grade hardware using only publicly available datasets. By releasing not only model weights but also using very affordable open-source hardware, SmolVLA aims to democratize access to vision-language-action models and accelerate research toward generalist robotic agents.

Despite using fewer than 30k training episodes—an order of magnitude less than other VLAs—SmolVLA matches or exceeds the performance of much larger models, both in simulation and the real world.

In a recent development, to make real-time robotics easier to use, we introduce an asynchronous inference stack. This technology separates how robots perform actions from how they understand what they see and hear. Because of this separation, robots can respond more rapidly in fast-changing environments.

SmolVLA is not only a lightweight yet capable model, but also a method for training and evaluating generalist robotics policies. In this section, we introduce the model architecture behind SmolVLA and the asynchronous inference setup used for evaluation, which has proven to be more adaptable and capable of faster recovery.

SmolVLA consists of two core components: a Vision-Language Model (VLM) that processes multimodal inputs and an action expert that outputs robot control commands. Below, we share the details of the main components of SmolVLA architecture and the Asynchronous Inference. More details can be found in our technical report.

Recent findings suggest that we use SmolVLM2 as our VLM backbone. It’s optimized for multi-image inputs and consists of a SigLIP vision encoder and a SmolLM2 language decoder.

It has been revealed that the decoder layers process concatenated image, language, and state tokens. The resulting features are then passed to the action expert.

SmolVLA’s action expert is a compact transformer (~100M parameters) that generates action chunks, i.e. sequences of future robot actions, conditioned on the VLM’s outputs. It is trained using a flow matching objective, which teaches the model to guide noisy samples back to the ground truth. In contrast, while discrete action representations (e.g., via tokenization) are powerful, they often require autoregressive decoding, which is slow and inefficient at inference time. While flow matching allows direct, non-autoregressive prediction of continuous actions, enabling real-time control with high precision.

More intuitively, during training, we add random noise to the robot’s real action sequences and ask the model to predict the “correction vector” that brings them back to the correct trajectory. This forms a smooth vector field over the action space, helping the model learn accurate and stable control policies.

We implement this using a transformer architecture with interleaved attention blocks (see the figure 2), and reduce its hidden size to 75% of the VLM’s, keeping the model lightweight for deployment.

In a recent development, while combining a vision-language model with an action prediction module is a common design pattern in recent VLA systems—such as Pi0, GR00T, Diffusion Policy — we identified several architectural choices that significantly enhance the robustness and performance. In SmolVLA, we apply three key techniques: reducing the number of visual tokens, skipping upper layers in the VLM, and interleaving cross- and self-attention layers in the action expert.

In a recent development, high-resolution images improve perception but can significantly slow down inference. To strike a balance, SmolVLA limits the number of visual tokens to 64 per frame during both training and inference. For example, a 512×512 image is compressed into just 64 tokens, instead of 1024, using PixelShuffle as an efficient shuffling technique. While the underlying Vision-Language Model (VLM) was originally pretrained using image tiling for broader coverage, SmolVLA uses only the global image at runtime to keep inference lightweight and fast.

Rather than always relying on the final layer of the VLM—which can be expensive and sometimes suboptimal—we use features from intermediate layers. Prior work has shown that early layers often provide better representations for downstream tasks. In SmolVLA, the action expert only attends to VLM features up to a configurable layer NN during training, set to half the total layers. This halves the compute cost of both the VLM and the action expert, significantly speeding up inference with minimal performance loss.

Inside the action expert, attention layers alternate between:.

According to recent reports, we found that this interleaved design is both lighter and more effective than using full attention blocks. Models that rely only on CA or only on SA tend to sacrifice either smoothness or grounding.

In SmolVLA, CA ensures that actions are well-conditioned on perception and instructions, while SA improves temporal smoothness—especially critical for real-world control, where jittery predictions can result in unsafe or unstable behavior.

Modern visuomotor policies output action chunks—sequences of actions to execute. There are two ways to manage them:.

Our async stack decouples action execution from chunk prediction, resulting in higher adaptability, and the complete lack of execution lags at runtime. It relies on the following key mechanisms:.

We are really excited about releasing asynchronous inference because it guarantees greater adaptability and improved performance without changing the model. In short, async inference keeps the robot responsive by overlapping execution and remote prediction.

In a recent development, while vision and language models thrive on web-scale datasets like LAION, ImageNet, and Common Crawl, robotics lacks a comparable resource. There’s no “Internet of robots.” Instead, data is fragmented across robot types, sensors, control schemes, and formats—forming disconnected "data islands". In our previous post, we explored how this fragmentation could be resolved through open, collaborative efforts. Just as ImageNet catalyzed breakthroughs in computer vision by providing a large, diverse benchmark, we believe that community-driven robotics datasets can play the same foundational role for generalist robot policies.

SmolVLA is our first step toward that vision: It is pretrained on a curated mix of publicly available, community-contributed datasets designed to reflect real-world variation. Rather than optimizing for dataset size alone, we focus on diversity: a range of behaviors, camera viewpoints, and embodiments that promote transfer and generalization.

All training data used in SmolVLA comes from LeRobot Community Datasets , robotics datasets shared on the Hugging Face Hub under the lerobot tag. Collected in diverse settings, from labs to living rooms, these datasets represent an open, decentralized effort to scale real-world robot data.

Figure 4. A glimpse of the community dataset. Special thanks to Ville Kuosmanen for creating the visualization. Unlike academic benchmarks, community datasets naturally capture messy, realistic interactions: varied lighting, suboptimal demonstrations, unconventional objects, and heterogeneous control schemes. This kind of diversity will be very useful for learning robust, general-purpose representations.

We used a customfiltering tool created by Alexandre Chapin and Ville Kuosmanen to select datasets based on frame count, visual quality, and task coverage. After a meticulous manual review (special thanks to Marina Barannikov), we curated a collection of 487 high-quality datasets focused on the SO100 robotic arm, standardized at 30 FPS. This yielded around 10 million frames—at least one order of magnitude smaller than other popular benchmark datasets, yet significantly more diverse.

A common issue across community datasets was noisy or missing task descriptions. Many episodes lacked annotations or included vague labels like “task desc” or “Move”, “Pick”. To improve quality and standardize the textual input across datasets, we used Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct to generate concise, action-oriented descriptions.

Given sample frames and the original label, the model was prompted to rewrite the instruction in under 30 characters, starting with an action verb (e.g., “Pick,” “Place,” “Open”).

In a recent development, another challenge was inconsistent camera naming. Some datasets used clear names like top or wrist.right, while others used ambiguous labels like images.laptop, which varied in meaning. To fix this, we manually went through the datasets and mapped each camera view to a standardized scheme: OBS_IMAGE_1: Top-down view OBS_IMAGE_2: Wrist-mounted view OBS_IMAGE_3+: Additional viewpoints.

Industry observers note that we further isolate the contributions of community dataset pretraining and multitask finetuning. Without pretraining on the LeRobot community datasets, SmolVLA initially achieves 51.7% success on SO100. After pretraining on community-collected data, performance jumps to 78.3%, a +26.6% absolute improvement. Multitask finetuning further boosts performance, showing strong task transfer capabilities even in low-data regimes.

Recent findings suggest that finally, we evaluate SmolVLA under synchronous and asynchronous inference modes. Async inference decouples action execution from model inference, allowing the policy to react while the robot is moving.

This results in more responsive and robust real-world performance, especially in dynamic environments with shifting objects or external disturbances.

Industry observers note that smolVLA is our contribution to building robotics foundation models that are open, efficient, and reproducible. Despite its small size, it matches or outperforms larger, proprietary models across a range of real-world and simulated tasks. By relying solely on community-contributed datasets and affordable hardware, SmolVLA lowers the barrier to entry for researchers, educators, and hobbyists alike. But this is just the beginning. SmolVLA is more than just a model — it's part of a growing open-source movement toward scalable, collaborative robotics.

It has been revealed that together, we can make real-world robotics more capable, more affordable, and more open. ✨.

arXiv:2611.34414v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Coding agents are increasingly capable of generating 3D models, yet enabling consumers to effectively control the modeling process remains challenging. Existing workflows rely primarily on text prompts and reference images, which often struggle to convey precise spatial intentions and require iterative corrections. We introduce SemProxy, a lightweight intermediate representation that bridges intuitive human interaction and agentic 3D modeling. Instantiated as labeled 3D bounding boxes, semantic 3D proxies allow users to directly specify object parts and spatial arrangements while leaving geometric details to coding agents. These proxies can be serialized into structured text and rendered as images, making them directly accessible to existing coding agents without additional training or modifications. We further develop ProxyStudio, a user interface that integrates text, image references, and interactive 3D proxy editing into agentic modeling workflows. We demonstrate the versatility of SemProxy across object- and scene-level modeling tasks with different coding agents, and evaluate its effectiveness in supporting controllable human-agent collaborative 3D modeling through a user study.

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.34398v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Skill acquisition alone does not establish a reusable skill library: task proficiency does not specify a compositional interface. Motivated by agents that acquire and refine skills, we study independently learned soft-prompt skills on frozen language models, with skill identities and execution order supplied. Across four digit-task bases and three record-editing models, mean composition accuracy in one call is at most 7.6%, compared with 88.2% to 100% over two calls that add computation and an explicit intermediate output. Neutral-insertion training improves robustness but leaves substantial interference, which block length and per-token norm alone cannot explain on two of four digit bases. Blocks of the same operation need not be interchangeable: after training next to frozen learned partners, a post hoc test on two Qwen bases shows that replacing those partners with independently learned blocks of the same operations lowers median composition accuracy from 98.0% and 95.3% to 12.7% and 0.5%, although every replacement scores at least 90% alone. Repair can improve a composition while impairing the original skill, and rehearsal improves retention while transfer remains limited on Qwen2.5-0.5B. Internal interventions constrain explanations without identifying a shared failure mechanism. These findings motivate evaluating compatibility, retention and transfer alongside acquisition when building skill libraries for self-evolving agents. Code is available at https://github.com/YanLin-Quinne/SkillCompatibility.

arXiv:2611.34366v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Data management systems organize large text collections for tasks such as finding relevant studies and extracting contract clauses. Systems make long documents searchable by splitting them into independently indexed chunks. Chunking can separate text from its identifying details. The indexing challenge is to keep each chunk independently searchable while preserving the context needed to find and rank it. Existing methods either encode that context in chunk vectors or attach it as a text prefix. Context encoded only in vectors is unavailable to text rerankers. Prompted prefixes serve both vector search and reranking, but are costly to generate at indexing time and can underperform contextual encoders. We propose ConTra (Context That Travels), a reinforcement learning framework for training lightweight prefix generators. Its reward combines feedback from frozen embedding and reranking models with factual verification and length control. ConTra generates one prefix per chunk during index construction and stores the augmented text and its embedding for reuse across queries. To evaluate contextual retrieval across workloads and under interference, we introduce RealContextBench, a benchmark with five application collections and three controlled conditions that isolate the effect of distracting text. On ConTEB and RealContextBench, ConTra-2B outperforms the prompted 9B baseline using Anthropic's method and the PPLX-4B contextual encoder, with a margin of up to 3.15 points over their best overall scores, while indexing short documents 7.74 times and 2.15 times as fast as those baselines, respectively. Post-trained only on ConTEB, it leads the standalone methods on RealContextBench after reranking and is less sensitive than the prompted 2B baseline to random and topically similar distractors. Code, datasets, and trained models are available at https://github.com/SStan1/ConTra.

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.34351v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Computational modeling of behavior represents individuals with a model fitted to their observed behavior and characterizes them through its parameters. Naturalistic tasks incorporate the complexity of real environments and yield high-dimensional behavioral trajectories. Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) infers the latent reward function underlying these trajectories. Standard IRL, however, assumes effectively infinite-horizon planning, whereas human foresight is both bounded and state-dependent. Here we introduce SC-AIRL (State-Conditional Adversarial IRL), which builds these two cognitive properties into the planner. Per-depth policies share one reward but differ in how far ahead they sum it explicitly. A state-conditional router mixes them according to the current state. Across held-out episodes in pedestrian crossing and highway overtaking tasks, SC-AIRL improves imitation over Standard AIRL, raising top-1 accuracy from 0.549 to 0.647 and from 0.629 to 0.718, respectively, while more closely reproducing participant behavior in rollouts. Inferred planning depth correlates with self-reported anxiety and motor impulsivity. SC-AIRL thus reproduces human behavior more closely than Standard AIRL while providing an interpretable, model-derived measure of state-dependent foresight.

arXiv:2611.34331v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce Puzzling-Bench, a benchmark of 23,777 puzzles with community-verified answers drawn from the Puzzling Stack Exchange archive (2014-2026): riddles, ciphers, logic grids, lateral-thinking problems, wordplay and recreational mathematics, a third of them with images. Every puzzle carries the answer accepted by its author, a short reference answer taken from it (LLM-extracted for the evaluation sets and checked on a 50-puzzle human review), the author's own hints, community tags and a creation date, so that the benchmark supports hint ablations, category analysis and a rolling post-cutoff slice (254 puzzles posted after the training cutoff of six of the nine models we evaluate, including the best one) as a contamination check. We evaluate nine frontier and open models with a two-tier scorer (normalized exact match, then an LLM judge) and validate the judge with three judges from two model families: they agree on 95-97% of verdicts (kappa 0.82-0.96), move no model by more than 1.6 points, and show no own-family preference. The best model, GPT-6.1, reaches 74.8% on a shared 255-puzzle set; a hard core of 17 puzzles defeats all nine models; model failures are strongly correlated, and the second-best model contributes a single puzzle to a greedy ensemble, yet an oracle over all nine reaches 91%. On a 100-puzzle multimodal pilot, withholding the question's image costs the two best models 24 and 35 points. We release the dataset, the scoring pipeline and all per-row provenance.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, at H Manufacturer, we are releasing Holo1, a family of Action Vision Language Models (VLMs) and WebClick, a latest multimodal localization benchmark on the Hugging Face Hub.

Surfer-H, a web-native agent that interacts with browsers like a human relies on the Holo1.

According to recent reports, holo1 is the first family of open-source Action VLMs designed specifically for deep web UI understanding and precise localization. The family includes Holo1-3B and Holo1-7B models, with the latter achieving 76.2% average accuracy on common UI localization benchmarks—the highest among small-size models. Industry observers note that web automation represents one of AI's most practical applications for businesses, but until now, solutions have often sacrificed cost-efficiency for performance. Surfer-H relies on the Holo1 family of open-weights models. It is a modular architecture for complete web task automation, which performs reading, thinking, clicking, scrolling, typing, and validating. It is designed to be flexible and modular, composed of three independent components: a Policy model that intends and drives the agent's behavior, a Localizer model that understands visual UIs for precise interactions, and a Validator model that confirms whether tasks are completed successfully. Unlike other agents that rely on custom APIs or brittle wrappers, Surfer-H operates purely through the browser — just like a real user.

Together, these solutions represent a fresh frontier in web automation, achieving state-of-the-art localization performance and setting the Pareto frontier in cost-efficient web navigation on the WebVoyager benchmark:.

We studied this in a repeated three-player majoritarian bargaining game with 2,234 participants. Players saw each opponent identified as Human or AI. The instructions described AI as acting either independently or on behalf of a human. Human participants made every decision. In mixed groups, players presented as AI received fewer points in opening offers, were included in fewer final agreements and earned about 18% less per round than those presented as Human. Smaller payoffs in agreements that included them accounted for most of the observed gap. Further analysis found a payoff gap even when all three players agreed. Social perceptions of AI may therefore shape who benefits from collective decisions, with potential costs for people represented by AI.

arXiv:2611.34298v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Random projection is a basic compression primitive for Euclidean representation learning, with the Johnson--Lindenstrauss lemma giving a target dimension $k=O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log n)$ independent of the ambient dimension. As hyperbolic representations gain increasing attention in modern Transformers, vision-language models, and large language models, the same need for oblivious dimensionality reduction arises, but no analogous primitive yet exists for hyperbolic representations. We study this gap. Two natural attempts fail in dual ways: a tangent-space scheme gives a clean local guarantee but is chart-bound and pays a curvature penalty, while a fully hyperbolic projection in the hyperboloid model is geometrically native but mixes radial and angular error before feeding them into the conditioning of $\operatorname{arcosh}$. We propose radial-angular random projection (RAP), which preserves the radial coordinate exactly and applies a Euclidean random projection only to the angular direction, lifting the result back to the target hyperboloid. RAP is hyperbolic-to-hyperbolic by construction, costs one Gaussian matrix-vector product, and reduces hyperbolic compression to a normalized angular JL question on $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$. We prove a finite-set RAP guarantee with explicit $\sinh(\sqrt{c}\,r_x)\sinh(\sqrt{c}\,r_y)$ conditioning, complemented by a local tangent-space JL theorem and an arcosh-conditioning lemma for the fully hyperbolic comparator. Across an origin-centered broad-radius point cloud, a balanced tree, a clustered Gaussian, and the WordNet noun hierarchy, RAP attains the lowest mean relative distortion in every $(n,k)$ cell, reducing distortion over the strongest hyperbolic baseline by approximately $48\%$--$49\%$ on broad-radius data. RAP also scales to million-point datasets and improves retrieval on vision--language representations over hyperbolic projection baselines.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • We have implemented KV Caching from scratch in our nanoVLM repository (a small codebase to train your own Vision Language Model with pure PyTorch).
  • Autoregressive language models generate text by sampling one token at a time.
  • This step-by-step generation is inherently sequential:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We have implemented KV Caching from scratch in our nanoVLM repository (a small codebase to train your own Vision Language Model with pure PyTorch). This gave us a 38% speedup in generation. In this blog post we cover KV Caching and all our experiences while implementing it. The lessons learnt are general and can be applied to all autoregressive language model generations. Implementing from scratch on a small codebase is a great learning experience, come along for the ride!

Autoregressive language models generate text by sampling one token at a time. During inference, the model processes a given input sequence, predicts the next token, appends it to the sequence, and repeats this process until some stopping criterion:.

This step-by-step generation is inherently sequential:.

This repetition also leads to computational redundancy. In this post, we explore KV Caching, an optimisation technique that mitigates this inefficiency.

Recent findings suggest that before diving into caching, let’s revisit how attention operates in transformer models. A Transformer language model consists of stacked layers, each composed of:.

To understand where KV Caching helps, we focus on the self-attention mechanism, specifically within a single attention head.

Let’s walk through a simple PyTorch implementation to visualise the key computations.

For a sequence of T T T input embeddings represented as X∈RT×D X \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times D} X∈RT×D, self-attention is computed as:.

Attention(X;Q,K,V)=softmax(QK⊤⋅Mdk)V \text{Attention}(X; Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left( \frac{QK^\top \cdot M}{\sqrt{d_k}} \right)V Attention(X;Q,K,V)=softmax(dk​​QK⊤⋅M​)V.

Here’s a minimal PyTorch equivalent using a causal mask:.

According to recent reports, in autoregressive generation, the model generates one token at a time. With each step, it recomputes Q Q Q, K K K, and V V V for the entire sequence, even though the earlier tokens haven’t changed.

These checks show that for all but the newest token, K K K and V V V are identical to previously computed values.

Recent findings suggest that most of the attention computation is repeated needlessly. This gets more expensive as sequences grow.

To eliminate this inefficiency, we use KV Caching:.

This changes generation from full-sequence re-computation to a lightweight, incremental enhancement.

✅ In practice, this cache is a per-layer dictionary with keys "key" and "value", each of shape (batch_size, num_heads, seq_len_cached, head_dim).

This is the foundation of how modern LLMs can generate long outputs efficiently.

Sources indicate that now that we understand the theory behind KV Caching, let’s see how it’s implemented in practice inside our nanoVLM repository. This is an ideal testbed, as it's a super concise and self-contained codebase.

KV caching is enabled across three key components in our model:.

In the LanguageModelGroupedAttention class, we modify the forward function to accept and update a cache of keys and values (block_kv_cache).

Sources indicate that previously, the model recomputed K K K and V V V at every generation step. Now we only compute Knew K_{\text{fresh}} Knew​, Vnew V_{\text{new}} Vnew​ for the current token, and append them to the cached values.

Sources indicate that in the LanguageModel class, we introduce layer-wise cache tracking. The start_pos argument helps the model compute correct rotary positional encodings for newly generated tokens.

The biggest architectural change is in the generate() method of the VisionLanguageModel.

We split generation into two stages:.

By separating these phases, we avoid redundant computation and dramatically speed up inference, especially for long prompts.

KV caching eliminates unnecessary computation during autoregressive generation, enabling faster and more efficient inference, especially in long sequences and real-time applications. This is a trade-off between speed and memory, and its drawbacks can be more complex code and restricting fancier inference schemes, like beam-search, etc. KV caching is a popular method for speeding up LLM inference, making it possible to run them on consumer hardware, and now you know how it works too!

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.34278v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: As large language models increasingly collaborate in heterogeneous multi-agent systems, latent communication has emerged as an efficient alternative to exchanging natural-language messages. By sharing internal representations, agents can avoid repeatedly processing the same context, reducing communication overhead and prefill computation. One such mechanism is cross-model Key-Value (KV) cache transfer, which uses a learned mapper to translate a source model's KV cache into one a target model can use. However, this handoff means the target model consumes context it did not encode itself, thus calling into question whether its safety alignment still holds. In this work, we investigate the security implications of latent handoffs by introducing Chasm, a framework characterizing cross-model handoff attacks across three fresh attack surfaces: the source model, mapper, and handoff mechanism itself. Our experiments reveal that latent handoffs substantially undermine safety alignment and prompt-injection defenses. Notably, a target model that follows only 0.4% of benchmark prompt injections natively, follows up to 44.2% when transferred through a mapper from a source model. On the other hand, for jailbreak attacks, transfer alone raises attack success by up to 24.6 pp within a model family and zero-shot attacks by up to 69.2 pp, whereas white-box optimization through the mapper boosts the attack success rate to 92.5%, against 37.5% for ordinary GCG on the same target. To address these vulnerabilities, we propose a lightweight target-side cache guard that corrects transferred caches to restore the target model's refusal, considerably mitigating these attacks.

arXiv:2611.34275v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) learns a response policy from human preference data, but with a limited dataset it can overfit to noisy or weakly informative preference labels. We introduce LatentCP-DPO, a framework that combines conformal prediction with pessimistic preference optimization for Bradley-Terry (BT) pairwise feedback and Plackett-Luce (PL) ranking feedback. Building on LatentCP's construction of uncertainty sets for unobserved model parameters, we address how to incorporate this uncertainty into preference optimization and characterize its effect on policy performance. Under exchangeability and a correctly specified preference model, we construct uncertainty sets for latent relative rewards with finite-sample marginal coverage from conformal prediction sets for observable preferences. We then learn a response policy by maximizing the worst-case expected preference log-likelihood over these uncertainty sets, using an independent collection of prompts and candidate responses without preference labels. Under suitable assumptions, we establish finite-sample upper bounds on regularized policy suboptimality that separate policy-class approximation error, conformal uncertainty, and statistical estimation error. For BT feedback, we further establish a worst-case lower bound for LatentCP-DPO that matches the upper bound's reciprocal dependence on the number of unlabeled optimization examples. The lower bound also reveals that the uncertainty sets can induce a bias that persists as the optimization sample grows. Together, these results characterize both the statistical accuracy and potential limitations of preference optimization using conformal uncertainty sets. Experiments support the benefits of the proposed framework in finite preference datasets.

Latest Update: ScreenSuite - The most comprehensive evaluation suite for GUI Agents!

📅 06 Jun 2025 | ⏱️ 4 min read (730 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over the past few weeks, we’ve been working tirelessly on making GUI agents more open, accessible and easy to integrate.
  • We are very excited to share it with you today: ScreenSuite is the most comprehensive and easiest way to evaluate Vision Language Models (VLMs)across many agentic capabilities!
  • In short, an AI Agent is a robot that acts in the virtual world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the past few weeks, we’ve been working tirelessly on making GUI agents more open, accessible and easy to integrate. Along the way, we created the largest benchmarking suite for GUI agents performances 👉 let us introduce ScreenSuite.

We are very excited to share it with you today: ScreenSuite is the most comprehensive and easiest way to evaluate Vision Language Models (VLMs)across many agentic capabilities!

GUI Agents in action - courtesy of OSWorld.

In short, an AI Agent is a robot that acts in the virtual world. (more thorough definition here).

In particular, a “GUI Agent” is an agent that lives in a GUI. Think “an agent that can do clicks and navigate on my desktop or my phone”, à la Claude Computer Use.

In a recent development, this means in essence that the AI model powering the agent will be given a task like “Fill the rest of this Excel column”, along with screen captures of the GUI. Using this information, it will then decide to take action on the system : click(x=130, y=540) to open a web browser, type(”Value for XYZ in 2025"), scroll(down=2) to read further… To see a GUI agent in action, you can try our Open Computer Agent, powered by Qwen2.5-VL-72B.

A good GUI agent will be able to navigate a computer just like we would, thus unlocking all computer tasks : scrolling through Google Maps, editing a file, buying an item online. This involves a variety of capabilities that can be hard to evaluate.

The literature, for instance Xu et al. (2025) or Qin et al. (2025), generally splits GUI agent abilities amongst several categories:.

So our first contribution is to gather and unify a comprehensive suite of 13 benchmarks spanning the full range of these GUI agent capabilities.

Recent findings suggest that if you look at the last category listed above, evaluating Multi-step agentic capabilities is especially challenging as it requires virtual machines to run the agent’s environment, be it Windows, Android, Ubuntu... To address this, we provide support both for E2B desktop remote sandboxes, and we created from scratch a new option to easily launch Ubuntu or Android virtual machines in Docker!

It has been revealed that we’ve carefully designed our benchmark suite with modularity and consistency in mind, ensuring strong alignment across tasks and environments. When required, especially for online benchmarks, we leverage smolagents as framework layer to streamline agent execution and orchestration.

To support reproducibility and ease of use, we’ve built custom Dockerized containers that allow local deployment of full Ubuntu Desktop or Android environments.

Sources indicate that unlike many existing GUI benchmarks that rely on accessibility trees or other metadata alongside visual input, our stack is intentionally vision-only. While this can result in different scores on some established leaderboards, we deem that it creates a more realistic and challenging setup, one that better reflects how humans perceive and interact with graphical interfaces.

– All agentic frameworks (Android World, OSWorld, GAIAWeb, Mind2Web) use smolagents and rely solely on vision, without any accessibility tree or DOM added (in contrast with evaluation settings reported in other sources). – Mind2Web (Multimodal) originally used element-name-based multi-choice selection based on the accessibility tree and screenshots, but was later adapted to click precision within bounding boxes using vision only, which significantly increases task difficulty.

We’ve evaluated leading VLMs on the benchmark.

Industry observers note that our scores are in general agreement with the scores reported in various sources! With the caveat that we evaluate on vision only, causing some differences, see implementation details above.

💡 Note that ScreenSuite does not intend to exactly reproduce benchmarks published in the industry: we evaluate models on GUI agentic capabilities based on vision. As a result, on benchmarks like Mind2Web where other benchmarks gave the agent a view of information rich context like DOM or accessibility tree, our evaluation setting is much harder, thus ScreenSuite does not match other sources.

The multistep benchmarks requires a bare-metal machine to run and deploy desktop/mobile* environment *emulators (see README.md).

Running consistent and meaningful evaluations easily allows the community to swiftly iterate and make progress in this field, as we’ve seen with Eleuther LM evaluation harness, the Open LLM Leaderboard and the Chatbot Arena.

We hope to see much more capable open models in the coming month that can run a wide range of tasks reliably and even run locally!

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.34230v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Deep learning models for prostate MRI segmentation often struggle to generalize when trained on limited heterogeneous data, leading to boundary errors and over-segmentation. We present an augmentation framework using mask-conditioned synthetic and diverse T2-weighted MRI volumes to improve boundary precision and reduce over-segmentation. We employ a 2.5D weakly mask-conditioned denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) via channel concatenation. The diffusion model conditions on stacks of adjacent binary masks from training folds. The model generates T2 volumes consistent with the conditioning anatomy while diversifying tissue appearance. We evaluate the proposed approach on two cohorts of data: (i) the LUND probe cohort (n=432) for strategy selection and training nnU-Net from scratch with a 23% synthetic data mix, and (ii) the Medical Segmentation Decathlon (MSD) prostate cohort (n=32) evaluated with a 20% synthetic data mix. For the LUND cohort, we found that training an nnU-Net model from scratch with a 23% synthetic data mix reduced the mean false-positive voxels per case from 11,102 (baseline) to 10,757. On the MSD cohort, the augmented model with a 20% synthetic mix achieved a mean cross-validated Dice of 0.9094, improving over the baseline (0.8935) by 1.59 percentage points and reducing mean false-positive voxels by 23.1% (4,201 to 3,229). Experimental results on both these cohorts suggest that mask-conditioned DDPM augmentation can reduce over-segmentation errors and improve boundary adherence in data-constrained settings.

Industry News: The Socratic PAUSE: safeguarding scientific judgement at AI speed

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (243 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.34222v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generative AI can turn a tentative scientific question into hypotheses, methods, code and interpretations within minutes. Yet generating a contribution does not establish that it deserves scientific reliance: researchers must still examine its evidence, assumptions and implications, and remain accountable for the decision to rely on it. Using Einstein's sketch of scientific discovery as a lens, we argue that AI has accelerated discovery far more than justification. In human-AI research partnerships, confidence can therefore outgrow evidence through three mechanisms: recursive reinforcement, loss of provenance and miscalibrated reliance on AI-generated contributions. Verification debt accumulates when such contributions are carried into later claims or decisions without adequate scrutiny. Accordingly, we propose the Socratic Pause as a deliberate checkpoint at consequential decision gates, where an AI contribution remains provisional while a researcher examines its basis. The PAUSE protocol structures this examination through five steps: Pin down the claim, Ask and challenge, Uncover assumptions and alternatives, Scrutinise the evidence and Exercise judgement. It concludes with a recorded decision to accept, revise, reject or defer the contribution. We show how AI research tools can support this practice without displacing human judgement, and outline a framework for evaluating whether it improves verification, decision-making and independent understanding. The aim is to preserve the freedom to explore with AI while ensuring that those responsible for the work can say what was examined, what remains uncertain and why the next step is justified.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today at GTC Paris, we are excited to announce Training Cluster as a Service in collaboration with NVIDIA, to make large GPU clusters more easily accessible for research organizations all over the world, so they can train the foundational models of tomorrow in every domain.

In a recent development, many Gigawatt-size GPU supercluster projects are being built to train the next gen of AI models. This can make it seem that the compute gap between the “GPU poor” and the “GPU rich” is swiftly widening. But the GPUs are out there, as hyperscalers, regional and AI-native cloud providers all quickly expand their capacity.

How do we then connect AI compute capacity with the researchers who need it? How do we enable universities, national research labs and companies all over the world to build their own models?

This is what Hugging Face and NVIDIA are tackling with Training Cluster as a Service - providing GPU cluster accessibility, with the flexibility to only pay for the duration of training runs.

To get started, any of the 250,000 organizations on Hugging Face can request the GPU cluster size they need, when they need it.

To get started, you can request a GPU cluster on behalf of your organization at hf.co/training-cluster.

Training Cluster as a Service integrates key components from NVIDIA and Hugging Face into a complete solution:.

Once your GPU cluster request is accepted, Hugging Face and NVIDIA will collaborate to source, price, provision and set up your GPU cluster per your size, region and duration requirements.

Training newly introduced AI models is a new path to predict the effect of pathogenic variants and for drug repositioning.

Tech Report: GeoCAM: Self-Supervised Sonar-Optical Representation Learning via Geographic Overlap Supervision

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (188 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.34218v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Cross-modal self-supervised learning for paired side-scan sonar and underwater optical imagery is a promising direction for benthic habitat understanding, but it remains underexplored because existing methods do not fully exploit the one-to-many correspondences and geographic metadata available in real opti-acoustic surveys. This limits the ability to learn representations that are both semantically meaningful and geometrically consistent from abundant unlabeled marine data. To address this problem, we present GeoCAM, a geography-guided framework that learns a shared embedding space for sonar tiles and their associated optical views without semantic annotations. GeoCAM achieves its goal by combining three components: (i) a Set Attention Aggregator that adaptively summarizes multiple optical observations into a single tile-level representation; (ii) a geometry-weighted InfoNCE objective that converts GPS-derived footprint overlap into soft positive supervision; and (iii) an optional cross-modal masked reconstruction branch that encourages physically grounded cross-modal alignment. Experiments on the BenthiCat SSS-CAM dataset show that GeoCAM can be effectively exploited to learn which sonar and camera samples describe the same seabed patch, improving cross-modal retrieval and alignment over strong contrastive baselines. Code is available at https://github.com/FadiZidiDz/GeoCAM.

Latest Update: Beyond Logits: Coherent Hallucination Mitigation via Attention Contrastive Decoding

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (144 words, ⚡ Quick Read) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.34207v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) demonstrate impressive multimodal capabilities, yet suffer from hallucination - generating factually inaccurate content. Contrastive Decoding (CD) mitigates this by contrasting amateur and expert branches at the logit level. However, our investigation reveals that such logit-level interventions fundamentally compromise generation coherence, necessitating restrictive penalty constraints unrelated to hallucination suppression. We introduce Attention Contrastive Decoding (ACD), a training-free plug-in that complements logit-level CD by relocating part of the contrastive operations to the attention mechanism. Operating at an earlier stage of the forward pass, ACD performs smooth semantic-preserving interventions through an Adaptive Subtraction Strategy (ASS), which attenuates hallucination-associated attention patterns while amplifying critical visual information. Extensive experiments demonstrate that combining ACD with existing CD methods (e.g., VCD+ACD) produces substantially more coherent outputs with further reduced hallucinations, eliminating restrictive penalties while enabling trustworthy multimodal generation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NVIDIA Isaac GR00T (Generalist Robot 00 Technology) is a research and development platform for building robot foundation models and data pipelines, designed to accelerate the creation of intelligent, adaptable robots.

Today, we announced the availability of Isaac GR00T N1.5, the first major upgrade to Isaac GR00T N1, the world’s first open foundation model for generalized humanoid robot reasoning and skills. This cross-embodiment model processes multimodal inputs, including language and images, to perform manipulation tasks across diverse environments. It is adaptable through post-training for specific embodiments, tasks, and environments.

In this blog, we’ll demonstrate how to post-train (fine-tune) GR00T N1.5 using teleoperation data from a single SO-101 robot arm.

Technical Blog for GR00T N1.5: https://research.nvidia.com/labs/gear/gr00t-n1_5/.

Now accessible to developers working with a wide range of robot form factors, GR00T N1.5 can be easily fine-tuned and adapted using the affordable, open-source LeRobot SO-101 arm.

This flexibility is enabled by the EmbodimentTag system, which allows seamless customization of the model for different robotic platforms, empowering hobbyists, researchers, and engineers to tailor advanced humanoid reasoning and manipulation capabilities to their own hardware.

Before proceeding to installation, please check if you satisfy the prerequisites.

arXiv:2611.34188v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Existing defenses against indirect prompt injection in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) are inherently reactive: prompt-engineering methods are often overridden by the injected instructions, while supervised detectors must be retrained for each newly introduced attack style. We propose a different paradigm: defend by maximizing relevance, not by detecting attacks. Our method, MINE, is training-free and attack-agnostic, and it also serves as a query-conditioned reranker. To evaluate defenses under realistic conditions, we introduce LC-Inj-SQuAD, a long-context benchmark with an average of 4,032 words per context. We evaluate on four datasets spanning short-context QA (Inj-SQuAD, Inj-TriviaQA), long-context QA (LC-Inj-SQuAD), and agent tool-call injection (InjecAgent). Across all four, MINE achieves the best accuracy--security trade-off among training-free defenses. It is also the only defense that stays usable against a fully adaptive attacker, generalizes to agent tool-call injection, and achieves the lowest inference latency on long contexts.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.34184v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multimodal sentiment analysis (MSA) in real-world systems must handle unpredictable modality missingness caused by sensor failures, privacy masking, and unstable transmission. Existing methods either learn reliability-aware representations or reconstruct missing inputs, often using a single flattened encoder output. This overlooks deep encoders' semantic hierarchy and intra- and inter-modal interactions, causing semantic averaging and ill-posed mappings. We propose Hierarchical Semantic Learning (HSL), a framework that exploits semantic hierarchy for robust MSA with missing modalities. Hierarchical Semantic Decoupling exposes low-, mid-, and high-level feature streams from each modality encoder. Cross-Modal Cross-Level Semantic Reconstruction performs ladder-style recovery, using high-level semantics from observed modalities as global anchors to progressively reconstruct mid-level structures and low-level details of missing modalities. To stabilize cross-level reconstruction, Hierarchical Cascade Error Supervisor applies prototypical contrastive regularization to observed and reconstructed features, enforcing level-specific semantic consistency and limiting error propagation. Finally, Hierarchical Interactive Fusion captures dense interactions across modalities and semantic levels to produce robust predictions under diverse missingness patterns. Experiments on CMU-MOSI, CMU-MOSEI, IEMOCAP, and CH-SIMS show that HSL outperforms baselines in most missing-modality settings.

arXiv:2611.34181v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision-language agents act on native-resolution renders of multi-element pages, where one perturbed photo or a few altered text strokes can redirect the decision. Any content provider can craft such a perturbation on the open model behind the agent, so a plug-in purifier is the natural first line of defense. Yet diffusion purifiers were designed and evaluated at the fixed resolution of the diffusion model on classifier or natural-image benchmarks, and defense evaluations for agents test JPEG, blur and noise but no diffusion purifier. We present the first study of adversarial purification at the agentic level, for an agent built on Qwen3-VL-8B: purifiers run at native resolution on multi-element inputs, face grey-box attackers who know the agent's model but not the defense, and are compared at matched clean cost. We show that treating agentic inputs as classifier inputs misleads both evaluation and design. Resizing the input to the resolution of the diffusion model, as existing purifiers do, raises the TextVQA clean cost of the Divide-and-Conquer purifier (DC) from 4.0 to 35.7 points. On web-shop pages, DC keeps 85.0% grey-box robust accuracy against web-hardened perturbations, where cheap input transformations at matched clean cost keep at most 40.0%, and this robustness comes from the global noise level: input-estimated masks and noise levels add none. These findings hold on a disjoint held-out set and on a second VLM and yield three requirements for defenses, we release the protocol.

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.34169v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Post-stroke aphasia is clinically heterogeneous, and conventional classifications may not capture differences in brain functional organisation. We tested whether resting-state and task-based functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) could identify neurophysiological subgroups alongside clinical assessment.Seventy-nine patients underwent unsupervised clustering using three fNIRS feature views: resting-state activity and connectivity, language-task activation, and rest-to-task connectivity reconfiguration. Similarity network fusion and spectral clustering integrated the views. Clinical and behavioural measures were excluded from clustering.Three clusters (n = 32, 17 and 30) were identified. This solution had the largest eigengap and was the only candidate significant after permutation testing and Holm correction (adjusted P = 0.001). It was stable under subsampling (mean adjusted Rand index, 0.773), but agreement fell to 0.217 when the resting-state view was removed. Clusters differed in most regional intrinsic-activity measures and all resting-state connectivity summaries, with few differences in task activation or connectivity reconfiguration. Their profiles showed higher right anterior prefrontal activity, distributed fronto-sensorimotor and parietal alterations, and reduced interhemispheric connectivity, respectively.Cluster membership was not significantly associated with conventional aphasia subtype (Cram\'er's V = 0.287), and baseline clinical language scores and task performance did not differ between clusters.These findings identify three neurophysiological subgroups distinguished mainly by intrinsic activity and resting-state functional connectivity, not clearly aligned with conventional aphasia classifications or baseline clinical measures. Multi-view fNIRS analysis may complement clinical characterisation, requiring independent and longitudinal validation.

arXiv:2611.34158v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Task allocation in contested-objective team games requires coordinated decisions under uncertainty, spatial constraints, and changing tactical conditions. In such settings, multiple agents must anticipate both teammate behavior and opponent actions. We study a hybrid predict-then-optimize approach for assigning controllable agents to objectives in real time. A masked multi-head model predicts tactical signals for each agent, including survival chance, local superiority, combat interaction, travel time, and objective contribution. These signals are combined with rule-based terms in a score matrix, and a minimum-cost flow solver computes coordinated global assignments constrained by capacity, occupancy, stability, and defensive strategies. Learning is limited to tactical scoring, while explicit rules and solver structure preserve controllability and interpretability. We evaluate the system using predictive metrics, offline assignment diagnostics, online A/B evaluation, and latency measurements. The system is an R\&D research prototype built on a commercial game and is not deployed in the shipped game. The results indicate that learned tactical estimates can support stable, feasible, and inspectable objective allocation under strict real-time constraints.

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.34152v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) excel at static visual understanding and are increasingly applied to spatial planning, where a model interprets a visual layout and outputs an action sequence to reach a goal. Grid games are a common testbed for this ability because their rules are explicit and a solver can verify every move. Yet existing benchmarks mostly report end-to-end success rates, which hide whether a failure stems from visual perception, rule application, or multi-step planning. We introduce GridProbe, a diagnostic benchmark that 1) locates the failing stage between visual perception and planning and 2) verifies the diagnosis by targeted fine-tuning. On Sokoban, GridProbe pairs end-to-end solving with four probes (recognition, localization, single-step prediction, and state tracking) and gives every board both as an image and as an equivalent text grid. Evaluating seven MLLMs on Sokoban and a maze game reveals distinct bottlenecks behind similar success rates: proprietary models are limited by multi-step planning, whereas open-source models are limited by rule application or by visual grid indexing, i.e., counting rows and columns. Planning failures also hide perception failures: when planning is easier, the visual cost of the same model grows from 7.6 to 37.7 points. The diagnosis identifies what to train: fine-tuning only the vision module of the perception-limited model on board reading raises its interactive Sokoban success 3.5-fold (5.8% to 20.4%) and transfers zero-shot to the unseen maze game (single-turn success 13.8% to 67.1%), whereas the same data does not help a rule-limited model and training on solver solutions brings no gain. We will release the benchmark and code at https://github.com/suat-llm/GridProbe.

Reproducer Synthesis for AI-Reported Bugs in the Linux Kernel

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (232 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.34142v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Agentic review systems are increasingly flagging suspected bugs in Linux kernel patches as textual reports. A maintainer who receives such reports needs further inspection to determine whether the report is true. The inspection requires understanding whether the bug can be triggered and, if necessary, manually constructing one. As a consequence, despite the excessive textual explanation, many reports go unanswered. In this paper, we argue that a runnable proof-of-concept (PoC) is the key information in such AI-generated kernel review reports. It is, however, challenging to automatically synthesize a valid and runnable PoC. We present ReproCue, a framework that generates PoCs for AI-generated Linux kernel reviews. ReproCue replays the historical kernel bugs and learns one reproduction finite-state-machine (FSM) per subsystem from successful runs. An FSM records the steps a reproduction goes through, together with the requirements observed at each step. Given a fresh review, ReproCue follows the FSM of that subsystem, adjusting the PoC and the environment as execution reveals what is missing. In 100 recent AI-generated reviews, ReproCue writes PoCs for 49 of them, compared with 10 for the current agentic reproducer and 9 for the state-of-the-art directed fuzzing. Excitingly, with our generated PoCs, Linux kernel maintainers confirmed 69.4% of them, much higher than 9.3% from Sashiko where only textual explanations are included, making AI reviews more actionable in practice.

Think of it like the Model Hub, but for low-level, high-performance code snippets (kernels) that accelerate specific operations, often on GPUs.

Sources indicate that examples include advanced attention mechanisms (like FlashAttention for dramatic speedups and memory savings). Custom quantization kernels (enabling efficient computation with lower-precision data types like INT8 or INT4). Specialized kernels required for complex architectures like Mixture of Experts (MoE) layers, which involve intricate routing and computation patterns. As well as activation functions, and normalization layers (like LayerNorm or RMSNorm).

Instead of manually managing complex dependencies, wrestling with compilation flags, or building libraries like Triton or CUTLASS from source, you can use the kernels library to instantly fetch and run pre-compiled, optimized kernels.
